Installing barRoso
The barRoso package is available on GitHub and can be installed using devtools. Before installation, make sure you have the following packages installed:

devtools
LCVP
lcvplants

install.packages("devtools")

# Install dependencies
devtools::install_github("idiv-biodiversity/LCVP")
devtools::install_github("idiv-biodiversity/lcvplants")

# Install barRoso
devtools::install_github("DBOSlab/barRoso")

title: std_place
text:
barRoso::std_place()


Description
Cleans and standardizes the geographic columns of a biodiversity collection dataset. This includes unifying column names and harmonizing values for continent, country, stateProvince, county, municipality, and locality. The function handles translations, synonyms, upper-case anomalies, ISO country codes, and common geographic aliases.


Details
This function is used internally by the barRoso package to support record reconciliation, duplicate detection, and label generation across different biodiversity databases. It ensures consistency of location fields by correcting common mistakes and variations. Country names are translated to English and harmonized using countrycode Brazilian and U.S. state abbreviations are expanded to full names. Words for municipality in county and municipality, e.g. "Manaus Mun.", "Mun. de Castelo", "Município de Mucugê" or "Arriaga Municipio", are removed, leaving just the name.


Arguments







Argument
Description




df
A data frame containing biodiversity records.


colname_continent
Column name for continent (default: "continent").


colname_country
Column name for country (default: "country").


colname_stateProvince
Column name for state or province (default: "stateProvince").


colname_county
Column name for county (default: "county").


colname_municipality
Column name for municipality (default: "municipality").


colname_locality
Column name for locality (default: "locality").


rm_original_column
Logical; if TRUE, original columns are removed after cleaning (default: TRUE).





Value
A data frame with standardized geographic information. If rm_original_column = FALSE, the original columns are retained with *Original suffixes.


Examples
df <- read.csv("herbarium_records.csv")
df_clean <- std_place(df,
                      colname_country = "pais",
                      colname_stateProvince = "estado",
                      rm_original_column = FALSE)

title: barroso_std
text:
barRoso::barroso_std()


Description
A wrapper function that performs integrated cleaning and standardization of biodiversity collection records using the barRoso package. This includes harmonizing taxonomic, geographic, collector, and type status information, as well as flagging or removing unvouchered and duplicate specimens. Determiner names in identifiedBy are standardized with the same rules of collector names.


Details
This function orchestrates several std_* functions from the barRoso package to clean records from virtual herbaria and biodiversity portals. It handles multilingual field names, missing data, inconsistent formatting, and dataset chunking for large inputs. The function also detects and optionally removes duplicate records and specimens lacking voucher information.


Arguments







Argument
Description




…
Input data frame containing raw biodiversity records.


unvouchered
Logical; if TRUE, remove records of wood, seed, fruit, pollen and spirit collections (e.g. "INPAw", "INPA-Carpoteca"), and observations without a specimen (basisOfRecord like "HUMAN_OBSERVATION") (default: TRUE).


delunkcoll
Logical; if TRUE, removes records with unknown collectors (default: FALSE).


flag_missid
Reserved for future use. Currently not implemented.


flag_duplicates
Logical; if TRUE, flags duplicates with a logical column (default: TRUE).


rm_duplicates
Logical; if TRUE, removes duplicate specimens (default: FALSE).


colname_recordedBy
Column name for collector names.


colname_recordNumber
Column name for collector number.


colname_identifiedBy
Column name for determiner names. The column is standardized with std_identifiedBy() only when present in the data.


colname_continent
Column name for continent.


colname_country
Column name for country.


colname_stateProvince
Column name for state/province.


colname_county
Column name for county.


colname_municipality
Column name for municipality.


colname_locality
Column name for locality.


colname_collectionCode
Column name for collection code.


colname_institutionCode
Column name for institution code.


colname_typeStatus
Column name for type status.


colname_family
Column name for family.


colname_genus
Column name for genus.


colname_specificEpithet
Column name for specific epithet.


rm_original_column
Logical; if TRUE, remove original columns after standardization.





Value
A fully cleaned and standardized data frame ready for downstream reconciliation, duplicate handling, and label generation.


Examples
df <- read.csv("raw_herbarium_data.csv")
df_std <- barroso_std(df,
                      colname_country = "pais",
                      colname_stateProvince = "estado",
                      rm_duplicates = TRUE)

title: std_recordedBy
text:
barRoso::std_recordedBy()


Description
Cleans and standardizes the recordedBy and recordNumber fields in biodiversity collection data, consolidating collector names and removing inconsistencies across herbarium records. The function identifies and formats collector initials, extracts main collector names, and handles multilingual and complex name structures including multiple collectors, Asian unicode names, and Brazilian surname conventions.


Details
This function is part of the barRoso package. It supports reconciliation of biodiversity records, especially for resolving collector name discrepancies across duplicate specimens. A new column addCollector is created when multiple collectors are detected, storing secondary collectors as "et al.". Original columns can be preserved or overwritten.
Specifically, this function performs extensive string cleaning including:

Converting Chinese names written as unicode escapes (e.g. "<U+674E><U+5149><U+7167>") into abbreviated Latin names, as Chinese authors cite themselves (e.g. "G. Z. Li")
Parsing and normalizing collector names split by &, and, e, y, ;, |, etc.
Handling cases of one, two, or more collectors
Cleaning spacing, punctuation, and known collector aliases
Adding standardized initials or removing redundant suffixes (e.g., “et al.”)



Arguments







Argument
Description




df
A data frame containing biodiversity records.


colname_recordedBy
Column name for the main collector (default: “recordedBy”).


colname_recordNumber
Column name for the collector number (default: “recordNumber”).


rm_original_column
Logical; if TRUE, original columns are removed after cleaning. If FALSE, they are retained with *Original suffixes (default: FALSE).





Value
A data frame with cleaned and harmonized collector name fields. A new column addCollector is added where additional collectors are identified.


Examples
df <- read.csv("herbarium_records.csv")
df_clean <- std_recordedBy(df,
                           colname_recordedBy = "coletor",
                           colname_recordNumber = "num_coleta",
                           rm_original_column = FALSE)

title: barroso_dwc
text:
barRoso::barroso_dwc()


Description
Formats a dataset of herbarium records into Darwin Core column names and value formats, so that records downloaded from different sources, such as GBIF, speciesLink, REFLORA and JABOT, can be combined and standardized together.


Details
The source of the dataset is recognized from its columns and values, or can be given in source. Then:

Columns named as Darwin Core terms in other cases, e.g. recordedby or decimallatitude, are renamed into the terms, e.g. recordedBy and decimalLatitude, for any source.
speciesLink: the columns of the older speciesLink format are renamed into Darwin Core terms, e.g. collector into recordedBy, collectornumber into recordNumber, latitude into decimalLatitude, and species (just the epithet) into specificEpithet; spp (the binomial) becomes species, as in GBIF. The year, month and day of identification become dateIdentified; the author is added to scientificName; dates like "23/11/2011" become "2011-11-23"; and a missing recordNumber is taken from fieldNumber.
REFLORA (as returned by refloraR): the determiner "Administrador" (the system user, given to most records) becomes NA; dates like "11/10/2006" become "2006-10-11"; type status in Latin like "ISOTYPUS" becomes "isotype"; and the institution of RB becomes "JBRJ", as in GBIF and JABOT.
JABOT (as returned by jabotR): dates like "2008-9-26" or "22/4/2020" become "2008-09-26" and "2020-04-22".
GBIF: downloads are already in Darwin Core, so only the column names are checked.

In all sources, a binomial species column is created from genus and specificEpithet when missing, as in GBIF downloads. Columns that are not Darwin Core terms are kept unchanged.
By default, all columns are returned as character. Downloads of the same source may otherwise have different column types, e.g. coordinatePrecision as integer in a species with values and as character in a species without them, as in the speciesLink API used by plantR::rspeciesLink(), and then they cannot be combined with dplyr::bind_rows().
barroso_cat() runs this function on each source before combining them.


Arguments







Argument
Description




df
A data frame of biodiversity records.


source
The source of the records: "auto" (default) to recognize it from the data, or one of "speciesLink", "REFLORA", "JABOT" or "GBIF".


as_character
Logical; if TRUE (default), all columns are returned as character, so the outputs of different downloads can always be combined.


verbose
Logical; if TRUE, reports the source and what was changed.





Value
The data frame with Darwin Core column names and value formats.


Examples
splink <- data.frame(collector = "Queiroz, L. P.", collectornumber = "1350",
                     collectioncode = "HUEFS", genus = "Ormosia", species = "arborea",
                     scientificname = "Ormosia arborea",
                     scientificnameauthor = "(Vell.) Harms",
                     yearidentified = "2005", monthidentified = "3",
                     dayidentified = NA, latitude = "-12.97", longitude = "-38.5")
barroso_dwc(splink)

title: std_collection
text:
barRoso::std_collection()


Description
Cleans and standardizes herbarium acronyms in biodiversity datasets by harmonizing values from the collectionCode and institutionCode fields. The function corrects common issues in GBIF and other aggregated records, replacing ambiguous or placeholder codes with the herbarium acronyms of Index Herbariorum.


Details
This function is part of the barRoso package. Instead of a dictionary of every code, it uses regular expressions that generalize across datasets, in the following order:

Aggregated collections like "Tropicos" or "MO-Duplicates" are replaced with the herbarium of the specimen given in institutionCode (e.g. "NY"), or with "MO" when it is missing.
Generic words like "Botany", "Herbarium", "Vascular Plants" or "PNGplants" are replaced with the acronym in institutionCode or, when missing, with the acronym at the beginning of catalogNumber (e.g. "U.1317533" into "U") or in occurrenceID (e.g. "urn:catalog:INB:...").
Names of collections, like "F-Seedplants", "BHCB-Fanerogamas", "INPA-Carpoteca", "R-Tipos", "UIS-H" or "BSMvplantscoll", are reduced to the herbarium acronym. Codes of wood collections, like "INPAw", are kept, as they are Index Herbariorum codes.
Names of herbaria and institutions, like "Herbario INPA", "Herbario Nacional de Costa Rica (CR)" or "Instituto de Botanica de Sao Paulo", are replaced with the acronym given in the name or with the known acronym.
Codes that are not acronyms, like observation projects ("Observations", "Dados de Pesquisa SISBio"), companies ("Ecopetrol S.A") or numbers, are replaced with the acronym in institutionCode or catalogNumber, or with NA.

The columns catalogNumber and occurrenceID are used when present.


Arguments







Argument
Description




df
A data frame with biodiversity specimen records.


colname_collectionCode
Name of the column containing collection codes (default: "collectionCode").


colname_institutionCode
Name of the column containing institution codes (default: "institutionCode").


rm_original_column
Logical; if TRUE, original columns are removed after cleaning (default: TRUE).





Value
A data frame with standardized collection codes in the collectionCode column. If rm_original_column = FALSE, the original values are saved with a *Original suffix.


Examples
df <- data.frame(collectionCode = c("Tropicos", "Botany", "F-Seedplants",
                                    "Herbario INPA", "Observations"),
                 institutionCode = c("NY", NA, "F", "INPA", "iNaturalist"),
                 catalogNumber = c("100595392", "U.1317533", "V0059731F",
                                   "123", "340214363"))
std_collection(df)$collectionCode

title: std_identifiedBy
text:
barRoso::std_identifiedBy()


Description
Cleans and standardizes the identifiedBy field in biodiversity collection data, using the same name-cleaning rules of std_recordedBy(). Each determiner name is formatted with abbreviated initials before the surname (e.g. "Cardoso, D.B.O.S." into "D. B. O. S. Cardoso").


Details
Unlike std_recordedBy(), no additional column is created when there are several determiners. All names are kept in the same cell, each one standardized and joined as "D. Cardoso & L. P. Queiroz" or "A. Pott, V. J. Pott & D. Cardoso".
Before standardizing the names, the function removes information that often comes along with the determiner in the identifiedBy field, such as the prefix "det.", herbarium acronyms in parentheses (e.g. "(MO)"), and determination dates (e.g. "/VI-2011", ", 2006", "18 Jun 1996"). Missing or anonymous determiners are returned as NA.


Arguments







Argument
Description




df
A data frame containing biodiversity records.


colname_identifiedBy
Column name for the determiner (default: "identifiedBy").


rm_original_column
Logical; if TRUE, the original column is removed after cleaning. If FALSE, it is retained with the *Original suffix (default: FALSE).





Value
A data frame with the standardized determiner names.


Examples
df <- read.csv("herbarium_records.csv")
df_clean <- std_identifiedBy(df,
                             colname_identifiedBy = "identifiedBy",
                             rm_original_column = FALSE)

title: barroso_write_specimens
text:
barRoso::barroso_write_specimens()


Description
Writes the lists of examined specimens of one, several or all species of a database of herbarium records in Darwin Core format, as standardized by barroso_std(), into a Word (.docx) file, in the format of a botanical journal, e.g. Systematic Botany, Taxon, Kew Bulletin or Phytotaxa.


Details
The records are formatted with barroso_dwc(), so the columns may also come from other sources, e.g. speciesLink. The columns used are species, country, stateProvince, municipality, locality, decimalLatitude, decimalLongitude, minimumElevationInMeters, maximumElevationInMeters, day, month, year, reproductiveCondition, recordedBy, addCollector, recordNumber, collectionCode and catalogNumber; and, when present, the columns of barroso_flag_duplicates() with all herbaria of each specimen (duplicateCollectionCodes, duplicateCatalogNumbers). The author of each species comes from scientificNameAuthorship, acceptedScientificName or scientificName.
Duplicates of the same collection (same collector and number, or same collector, date and locality when there is no number) are written once, with all their herbaria. The specimens are ordered by country, state, municipality and date.
Examples of the format of each journal:

Nordic Journal of Botany: Ormosia arborea – Brazil, Bahia, Abaíra, Catolés, …, 8 May 1994, (fl), Cardoso et al. 2066 (HUEFS, RB). Mucugê, … Rodriguésia: Additional material examined: BRAZIL. BAHIA: Abaíra, Catolés, …, 8.V.1994, fl, D.B.O.S. Cardoso et al. 2066 (HUEFS, RB). Mucugê, …, A. Fernandes (EAC 11356).


Arguments







Argument
Description




df
A data frame of herbarium records in Darwin Core format, e.g. the output of barroso_std() or barroso_dwc(). Not needed when path is given.


path
Path to an .xlsx, .xls or .csv file with the herbarium records, used when df is NULL.


sheet
Sheet name or index of the .xlsx file. Default 1.


species
Character vector of species names, with or without authors (e.g. "Ormosia arborea"), to write the specimens of just these species. If NULL (default), the specimens of all species are written.


journal
Name of the journal whose format is followed, as in recent papers of the journal: "Systematic Botany" (default), "Acta Botanica Brasilica", "Annals of the Missouri Botanical Garden", "Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society", "Brazilian Journal of Botany", "Brittonia", "Candollea", "Edinburgh Journal of Botany", "Kew Bulletin", "Nordic Journal of Botany", "Phytotaxa", "PhytoKeys", "Plant Ecology and Evolution", "Rodriguesia", "Systematics and Biodiversity", "Taxon" or "Willdenowia". The name can be written in any case, with or without accents, and abbreviated (e.g. "systematic botany", "Kew", "Edinburgh", "Rodriguésia").


header
Text of the header before the specimens, e.g. "Additional specimens examined", "Paratypes" or "Selected specimens", written with the format and punctuation of the journal. If NULL (default), the header of the journal, e.g. "Representative Specimens Examined" in Systematic Botany. Use "" to write no header.


language
Language of the section header, months and countries: "en" (default) or "pt".


catalog_numbers
Logical. If TRUE, the catalog number is written after each herbarium, e.g. "(IAC no. 14754, NY no. 1162464)" in Brittonia. Default FALSE.


dir
Folder where the .docx file is saved. By default, the folder of path, or "results_specimens" when the records are given in df.


filename
Name of the .docx file. By default, the name of path (or "specimens") followed by the journal, e.g. "Ormosia_herbarium_records_Systematic_Botany.docx".


font_family
Font of the document. Default "Times New Roman".


font_size
Font size in points. Default 12.


verbose
Logical. Print progress messages. Default TRUE.





Value
Invisibly, a data frame with the species (species_name) and their examined specimens (specimens_text, one specimen per line). The .docx file is written as a side effect.


Examples
# All species of a database standardized by barRoso
barroso_write_specimens(path = "results/Ormosia_herbarium_records.xlsx",
                        journal = "Systematic Botany")

# Two species, in the format of Kew Bulletin
barroso_write_specimens(df = data_all_clean,
                        species = c("Ormosia arborea", "Ormosia fastigiata"),
                        journal = "Kew Bulletin",
                        dir = "results")

title: std_types
text:
barRoso::std_types()


Description
Cleans and standardizes the typeStatus column in biodiversity datasets, addressing inconsistencies in type designations. It removes irrelevant entries, harmonizes formatting, and optionally fills missing values if present in other duplicate records (assumed to be handled outside this function).


Details
This function is used internally in the barRoso package to prepare type status data for reconciliation and label generation. It corrects known placeholder or non-type entries (e.g. “Fotografia do Tipo”, “NOTATYPE”, “Epítipo”) and simplifies terms like "sim -" to ensure clean type labels.
The same type designation written in English, Latin or Portuguese, and in any case, is converted into the lowercase Darwin Core term in English, e.g. "ISOTYPE", "Isotypus" and "isótipo" into "isotype", "Parátipo" into "paratype", and "isosintipo" into "isosyntype". A taxon name after the term is kept, e.g. "ISOTYPUS of Ormosia amazonica Ducke" into "isotype of Ormosia amazonica Ducke".


Arguments







Argument
Description




df
A data frame containing type designation records.


colname_typeStatus
Name of the column holding type status information (default: "typeStatus").


rm_original_column
Logical; if TRUE, the original column is removed after cleaning (default: TRUE).





Value
A data frame with a standardized typeStatus column. If rm_original_column = FALSE, the original values are preserved in a column named typeStatusOriginal.


Examples
df <- read.csv("specimens.csv")
df_clean <- std_types(df,
                      colname_typeStatus = "tipo",
                      rm_original_column = FALSE)

title: News
text:
Initial Release
The first official release of the barRoso R package — a comprehensive toolkit for standardizing, harmonizing, and preparing plant specimen records for research and reconciliation.

Highlights

barroso_std(): Unified function to clean and standardize herbarium records across multiple fields (collector, geography, taxonomy, etc.).
barroso_flag_duplicates(): Flag potential duplicate specimens across herbaria using metadata patterns.
barroso_cat(): Combine and reconcile specimen records from multiple virtual herbaria (e.g., GBIF, SEINet, REFLORA, JABOT, speciesLink).
barroso_labels(): Generate printable herbarium labels from cleaned fieldbook data, with embedded maps and taxonomic authority retrieval.
Standardize collector names and collection numbers using regex-based parsing
Harmonize taxonomic, geographic, and temporal fields
Flag and remove potential duplicates across herbarium records
Generate herbarium labels from fieldbook data
Integrate with external taxonomic databases (e.g., LCVP, WFO)
Prepare large-scale biodiversity datasets for publication and analysis
Optimized for datasets from REFLORA, speciesLink, and JABOT.
Supports integration with tidyverse workflows for downstream analyses.
Test coverage >95%, continuous integration via GitHub Actions.



Philosophy
Unlike other tools that aggressively clean (and discard) records, barRoso focuses on standardization first — ensuring that all specimens, even misidentified or ambiguous ones, remain usable and discoverable. Standardization also enables better duplicate detection and data reconciliation without losing valuable information.


Infrastructure

MIT license.
GitHub Actions: R-CMD-check, test coverage, continuous integration.
Website: barRoso documentation site



Feedback
Please report bugs or feature requests here:
https://github.com/DBOSlab/barRoso/issues

title: barRoso
text:
Graziela Maciel Barroso
Graziela Maciel Barroso (1912–2003) was one of Brazil’s most influential botanists, with a 58-year career at the Rio de Janeiro Botanical Garden. She specialized in plant taxonomy and morphology, shaping how generations of scientists understand and classify Brazil’s flora. Her work was instrumental in developing identification keys and guides used in herbaria across Brazil and abroad.
She authored the landmark three-volume Sistemática de Angiospermas do Brasil (1978–1986), still a cornerstone of botanical education, as well as Frutos e Sementes – Morfologia Aplicada à Sistemática de Dicotiledôneas (1999). Beyond her scientific contributions, she was a committed educator and mentor, and a courageous advocate for science and democracy during Brazil’s military dictatorship.
Barroso remained professionally active until her passing at age 92. A month before her death, she was elected to the Brazilian Academy of Sciences, a distinction awarded posthumously.

title: Compare Herbarium Sources
text:
Overview
When working with plant specimen data from multiple biodiversity repositories (e.g., GBIF, JABOT, speciesLink), users often encounter overlapping records across sources. barRoso offers the barroso_cat() function to merge, harmonize, and optionally deduplicate these datasets based on collection codes.
This article demonstrates how to:

Merge multiple data sources into a unified data frame
Combine raw speciesLink downloads with GBIF downloads
Prioritize a preferred source when herbaria overlap

title: Compare Herbarium Sources
text:
Function: barroso_cat()
combined_df <- barroso_cat(
  list_sources = list(
    GBIF = gbif_data,
    speciesLink = splink_data,
    JABOT = jabot_data
  ),
  keep_source = "GBIF"
)

title: Compare Herbarium Sources
text:
Arguments

list_sources: A named list of data frames, one per biodiversity source. The names (e.g. GBIF, speciesLink) must be unique, as they are used to identify the source of each record.
keep_source: Optionally, the name of the preferred source (e.g. "GBIF"). The records of any herbarium also present in the preferred source are removed from the other sources.

If no source is specified, the function merges all sources, retaining potential duplicates for further reconciliation with barroso_flag_duplicates().

title: Compare Herbarium Sources
text:
Example
library(barRoso)

# Load datasets downloaded from GBIF and speciesLink
gbif <- read.csv("gbif.csv")
splink <- read.csv("speciesLink.csv", fileEncoding = "latin1")

# Merge, giving preference to GBIF for overlapping herbaria
combined_df <- barroso_cat(
  list_sources = list(
    GBIF = gbif,
    speciesLink = splink
  ),
  keep_source = "GBIF"
)

table(combined_df$datasource)
For example, when combining 9,806 GBIF records and 4,432 speciesLink records of Ormosia, 1,259 speciesLink records of 74 herbaria also available in GBIF are removed, resulting in 12,979 records (9,806 from GBIF and 3,173 from speciesLink).

title: Compare Herbarium Sources
text:
How It Works

1. Raw speciesLink columns are renamed into Darwin Core
Each source is first formatted with barroso_dwc(), which can also be used alone.
Raw speciesLink downloads use lowercase column names that differ from the Darwin Core terms used by GBIF. barroso_cat() detects them and renames them automatically, so records of both sources end up in the same columns:

In speciesLink, the column species is just the specific epithet (e.g. arborea), while in GBIF it is the binomial (e.g. Ormosia arborea). So the speciesLink species becomes specificEpithet, and a binomial species column is created, as in GBIF.


2. REFLORA and JABOT values are standardized
Records downloaded with refloraR and jabotR already have Darwin Core column names, but some of their values are written differently from GBIF. barroso_cat() recognizes these sources by their content, whatever their names in list_sources, and standardizes them:

library(refloraR)
library(jabotR)

reflora <- reflora_records(herbarium = c("RB", "K"), taxon = "Ormosia", save = FALSE)
jabot <- jabot_records(herbarium = c("MBM", "UPCB"), taxon = "Ormosia", save = FALSE)

combined_df <- barroso_cat(
  list_sources = list(GBIF = gbif, speciesLink = splink, REFLORA = reflora, JABOT = jabot),
  keep_source = "GBIF"
)
The REFLORA collection of RB is fed by JABOT, so the same RB specimens are often found in both sources, and also in GBIF. With keep_source = "GBIF", they are kept just once.


3. Overlapping herbaria are removed when keep_source is given
Overlapping herbaria are detected with collectionCode. When keep_source = "GBIF", the records of any herbarium present in GBIF are removed from the other sources. Herbaria shared only among the other sources (e.g. present in both speciesLink and JABOT, but not in GBIF) are kept in all of them, and their duplicates can then be flagged with barroso_flag_duplicates().


4. Columns are aligned

Columns missing in some sources are filled with NA.
Columns with different types across sources (e.g. year as numbers in GBIF and as text in speciesLink) are combined as text, instead of failing.
A new column datasource stores the source of each record (e.g. "GBIF", "speciesLink").

title: Compare Herbarium Sources
text:
Tips

Name each data source in list_sources, e.g. list(GBIF = gbif, speciesLink = splink)
Ensure each dataset includes a collectionCode column, otherwise overlapping herbaria cannot be detected for that source
Use keep_source = NULL if you want to preserve all records
Use barroso_std() after combining to clean the remaining fields and flag duplicates

cleaned_df <- barroso_std(combined_df, flag_duplicates = TRUE)

Overview
The barroso_labels() function generates printable herbarium labels directly from field book spreadsheets or CSV files. Labels include specimen information, taxonomic authority, formatted locality descriptions, and location maps (with greater resolution for USA-based collections).

title: Write Lists of Examined Specimens
text:
Overview
Taxonomic revisions and descriptions of new species cite the specimens examined for each species, in a format that differs from journal to journal: the header, the case and format (bold, italics, small capitals) of countries, states and collectors, how dates and coordinates are written, and how herbaria are listed.
The function barroso_write_specimens() writes these lists for one, several or all species of a database of herbarium records into a Word (.docx) file, in the format of a chosen journal. This article goes through the whole workflow with two R scripts, using the herbarium records of Luetzelburgia (Leguminosae), a genus of 15 species of South American trees:

01_get_standardized_records_script.R downloads the records from GBIF, REFLORA and JABOT, combines and standardizes them, and saves a spreadsheet;
02_write_examined_specimens_script.R writes the lists of examined specimens from this spreadsheet, in the format of several journals.

Both scripts are run from an RStudio project, e.g. build_herbarium_records_database, with the scripts in a folder scripts and the results saved in a folder results.

title: Write Lists of Examined Specimens
text:
Script 1: get standardized records
The records are downloaded with plantR (GBIF), refloraR (REFLORA Virtual Herbarium) and jabotR (JABOT, Rio de Janeiro Botanical Garden). The list of accepted species comes from Kew’s WCVP, with the package rWCVPdata.
# 01_get_standardized_records_script.R

library(barRoso)
library(refloraR)
library(jabotR)
library(plantR)
library(dplyr)
library(openxlsx)
library(rWCVPdata)

# Create a folder for the results of today
dir <- "results"
folder_name <- paste0(dir, "/", format(Sys.time(), "%d%b%Y"))
if (!dir.exists(folder_name)) dir.create(folder_name, recursive = TRUE)

# All accepted species of Luetzelburgia in WCVP
wcvp_names <- rWCVPdata::wcvp_names
luetz_wcvp <- subset(wcvp_names,
                     genus == "Luetzelburgia" &
                       taxon_rank == "Species" &
                       taxon_status == "Accepted")
luetz_list <- sort(luetz_wcvp$taxon_name)

# GBIF: one search for each species, skipping species without records
data_gbif <- lapply(luetz_list, function(x) {
  gbif <- tryCatch(plantR::rgbif2(species = x, n.records = 5000, force = TRUE,
                                  remove_na = FALSE, save = FALSE, compress = FALSE),
                   error = function(e) NULL)
  if (!is.data.frame(gbif) || nrow(gbif) == 0) return(NULL)
  gbif
})
names(data_gbif) <- luetz_list
data_gbif <- dplyr::bind_rows(data_gbif, .id = "original_search")

# REFLORA Virtual Herbarium
data_reflora <- refloraR::reflora_records(repatriated = TRUE, taxon = "Luetzelburgia",
                                          indets = TRUE, updates = TRUE,
                                          verbose = TRUE, save = FALSE)
unlink("reflora_download/", recursive = TRUE, force = TRUE)

# JABOT
data_jabot <- jabotR::jabot_records(taxon = "Luetzelburgia", indets = TRUE,
                                    updates = TRUE, verbose = TRUE, save = FALSE)
unlink("jabot_download/", recursive = TRUE, force = TRUE)

# Combine the sources, keeping GBIF for the herbaria present in more than one
records_list <- list(GBIF = data_gbif,
                     REFLORA = data_reflora,
                     JABOT = data_jabot)
data_all <- barRoso::barroso_cat(list_sources = records_list,
                                 keep_source = "GBIF")

# Standardize collectors, herbaria, places and taxa, and remove duplicates
data_all_clean <- barRoso::barroso_std(data_all,
                                       unvouchered = TRUE,
                                       delunkcoll = TRUE,
                                       flag_duplicates = TRUE,
                                       rm_duplicates = TRUE)

# Fix and flag coordinates
data_all_clean <- barRoso::std_coordinates(data_all_clean)

# Save the database
openxlsx::write.xlsx(data_all_clean,
                     paste0(folder_name, "/Luetzelburgia_herbarium_records.xlsx"))
In November 2026, this script found 3,215 records in GBIF, 1,093 in REFLORA and 351 in JABOT:
#> barroso_cat: removing 1089 records of 39 herbaria from REFLORA also present in GBIF
#> barroso_cat: removing 337 records of 10 herbaria from JABOT also present in GBIF
After the standardization, without duplicates, unvouchered records and records of unknown collectors, the database has 1,202 records of 15 species, from Brazil (1,155), Bolivia (35), Colombia (3) and Guyana (3).

title: Write Lists of Examined Specimens
text:
Script 2: write the examined specimens
The second script reads the spreadsheet saved by the first one, and writes one .docx file for each journal, in the same folder:
# 02_write_examined_specimens_script.R

library(barRoso)
library(openxlsx)

# The most recent spreadsheet within the results folder
dir <- "results"
records_files <- list.files(dir,
                            pattern = "^Luetzelburgia_herbarium_records[.]xlsx$",
                            recursive = TRUE,
                            full.names = TRUE)
records_file <- records_files[which.max(file.mtime(records_files))]
folder_name <- dirname(records_file)

# Read the records once, so the spreadsheet is not read again for each journal
data_records <- openxlsx::read.xlsx(records_file)

# One Word (.docx) file for each journal. To write just some species, use the
# argument species, e.g. species = c("Luetzelburgia andina", "Luetzelburgia harleyi")
journals <- c("Annals of the Missouri Botanical Garden",
              "Systematic Botany",
              "Kew Bulletin",
              "Rodriguesia")

for (journal in journals) {
  barRoso::barroso_write_specimens(
    df = data_records,
    species = NULL,
    journal = journal,
    dir = folder_name,
    filename = paste0("Luetzelburgia_examined_specimens_", gsub("\\s+", "_", journal))
  )
}
#> Skipping 5 records not identified to species
#> Examined specimens of 15 species (1131 specimens) written in the format of
#> Annals of the Missouri Botanical Garden to:
#> results/01Nov2026/Luetzelburgia_examined_specimens_Annals_of_the_Missouri_Botanical_Garden.docx
#> ...

title: Write Lists of Examined Specimens
text:
How the specimens are written

Columns. The function uses the Darwin Core columns species, country, stateProvince, municipality (or county, where GBIF keeps the municipalities of Brazil), locality, decimalLatitude, decimalLongitude, minimumElevationInMeters, maximumElevationInMeters, day, month, year, reproductiveCondition (phenology), recordedBy, addCollector, recordNumber, collectionCode, catalogNumber. Missing columns are just skipped.
Collectors. The names standardized by barroso_std() (e.g. D. B. O. S. Cardoso) are written as each journal cites them. The additional collector (addCollector) is written as et al. (& al. in Taxon) or as the name of the second collector, e.g. R.M. Harley & A.M. Giulietti.
Duplicates. Duplicates of the same collection (same species, collector surname and number, or same collector, date and locality when there is no number) are written once, with all their herbaria in alphabetical order, including those found by barroso_flag_duplicates() (duplicateCollectionCodes).
Types. The type status is not written, as types are cited apart from the examined specimens.
Collections without number. The catalog number of the first herbarium is written, e.g. R. Spruce s.n. (K000892474, LD), so that the specimen can be found. Use catalog_numbers = TRUE to write the catalog numbers of all herbaria.
Order. Specimens are ordered by country, state, municipality and date. Records not identified to species are skipped.
Species. For each species, a heading with the species name in italics and its author (from scientificNameAuthorship, acceptedScientificName or scientificName) is followed by the paragraph of its specimens.

The function returns, invisibly, a data frame with the species and their specimens, one per line, which can be checked in R:
res <- barroso_write_specimens(path = "results/01Nov2026/Luetzelburgia_herbarium_records.xlsx",
                               species = "Luetzelburgia andina", verbose = FALSE)
cat(res$specimens_text)

title: Write Taxonomic Descriptions
text:
Overview
The barroso_write_taxon_descr() function is a powerful tool in the barRoso package for generating automated morphological descriptions from structured Excel data. It transforms taxonomic and morphological character data into standardized, publication-ready species descriptions in Word document format.

title: Write Taxonomic Descriptions
text:
Key Features

Automatically generates species descriptions from morphological Excel data
Groups related characters and avoids term repetition
Combines measurements (length × width) with proper units and symbols
Formats measurement ranges with en dashes (e.g., “4.3–14.5 cm”)
Handles complex hierarchical character structures
Merges duplicate species entries intelligently
Customizable text formatting (bold, italic) for different description elements
Exports professionally formatted Word (.docx) documents

Usage
library(barRoso)

# Generate descriptions for all species
descriptions <- barroso_write_taxon_descr(
  xlsx_path = "morphological_data.xlsx",
  species_cols = c("Genus", "Species", "Author"),
  character_cols = 4:20
)

# Generate descriptions only for specific species
descriptions <- barroso_write_taxon_descr(
  xlsx_path = "morphological_data.xlsx",
  species_cols = c("Genus", "Species"),
  character_cols = 3:15,
  species_filter = c("Ouratea concinna", "Ouratea coarctata")
)

# Customize formatting and output
descriptions <- barroso_write_taxon_descr(
  xlsx_path = "morphological_data.xlsx",
  species_cols = 1:3,
  character_cols = 4:25,
  font_family = "Arial",
  font_size = 11,
  species_bold = TRUE,
  species_italic = TRUE,
  group_bold = FALSE,
  group_italic = TRUE,
  description_bold = FALSE,
  description_italic = FALSE,
  filename = "MySpeciesDescriptions",
  dir = "Output"
)

title: Flexible Column Names
text:
Overview
Herbarium datasets vary widely in how they name their columns. One dataset might label a column as estado, while another might use stateProvince or province. To make barRoso work with any data source, all standardization functions support flexible column naming.
The barroso_std() function accepts parameters such as colname_country, colname_stateProvince, colname_recordedBy, and more. These let you specify the actual column names in your input data.
This flexibility is essential when cleaning datasets from mixed sources like GBIF, speciesLink, JABOT, or SEINet.

title: Flexible Column Names
text:
Specifying Custom Column Names
Use named arguments in barroso_std() to point to your actual column names. For example:
library(barRoso)

# Assume your dataset uses "pais" and "estado" instead of "country" and "stateProvince"
df <- read.csv("raw_data.csv")

df_std <- barroso_std(df,
                      colname_country = "pais",
                      colname_stateProvince = "estado",
                      colname_recordedBy = "coletor",
                      colname_recordNumber = "numero",
                      colname_identifiedBy = "determinador",
                      colname_collectionCode = "herbario",
                      colname_institutionCode = "instituicao",
                      colname_locality = "localidade",
                      colname_family = "familia",
                      colname_genus = "genero",
                      colname_specificEpithet = "epiteto",
                      rm_duplicates = TRUE)
The standardized columns keep your names, and the original values are kept with the suffix Original, e.g. herbario and herbarioOriginal.
The individual functions accept the same arguments, e.g.:
df_std <- std_collection(df,
                         colname_collectionCode = "herbario",
                         colname_institutionCode = "instituicao",
                         rm_original_column = FALSE)

df_coords <- std_coordinates(df,
                             colname_decimalLatitude = "latitude",
                             colname_decimalLongitude = "longitude",
                             colname_country = "pais")

title: Flexible Column Names
text:
Why This Matters

Ensures compatibility with multilingual datasets
Prevents failure due to missing or misnamed columns
Helps merge and clean records from disparate herbaria

title: Flexible Column Names
text:
Recommendations

Always check the column headers of your CSV or data frame before calling barroso_std()
Rename fields only if necessary — using this feature gives you more flexibility

This makes barRoso highly generalizable for data standardization across any herbarium or biodiversity dataset.

title: Detect and Flag Duplicates
Detect and Flag Duplicates

How duplicates are found







Case
Records are duplicates when they share




With collector number
the collector (recordedBy) and the collector number (recordNumber)


Without collector number
the species name, the collector and the full collection date (year, month and day)




Records with unknown collector (NA or "Unknown") are never treated as duplicates, as "Unknown 1" in two herbaria are most likely different collections.
Without collector number, the full date is required, because the same collector may have collected the same species in different days.
The specific epithet is taken from specificEpithet or, when missing, from a binomial in the column species, as in GBIF downloads, which have no specificEpithet column.

The herbarium acronym is pasted before each catalog number, except when the catalog number already starts with it (e.g. RB00123, K000555). Records that are not duplicates also receive their own herbarium and catalog number in these two columns, so the columns are complete for the whole dataset.

Conflicting identifications
A block has identificationConflict = TRUE when its duplicates are identified as:

different species, e.g. Ormosia arborea and Ormosia nitida; or
different genera, e.g. Ormosia arborea and Swartzia apetala in block 1.

A duplicate identified just to genus does not conflict with a complete name of the same genus. That is why block 2, with Ormosia and Ormosia nitida, has no conflict: the genus-only record is just less complete.
Names are compared exactly, so spelling variants (e.g. Ormosia trifoliata and Ormosia trifoliolata) are also flagged. This helps finding misspelled names, besides misidentifications.

title: Detect and Flag Duplicates
text:
Removing duplicates
With rm_duplicates = TRUE, only one record per block is kept. The record is chosen by three rules, applied in this order. Each rule only chooses among the records that passed the previous one.
df_clean <- barroso_flag_duplicates(df, rm_duplicates = TRUE)

Rule 1: identified to species
Records with a complete species name (genus and specific epithet) are preferred over records identified just to genus.

Block 1: the RB duplicate (Ormosia) is discarded; MO, JBB, K and HUEFS go to rule 2.
Block 2: the ALCB duplicate (Ormosia) is discarded, even though it is the only one with coordinates; HUEFS (Ormosia nitida) is kept.

If all duplicates of a block are identified just to genus, all of them go to rule 2.


Rule 2: most frequent identification
Among the remaining records, those with the name given by most duplicates are preferred.

Block 1: Ormosia arborea is given by three duplicates (MO, JBB, HUEFS) and Swartzia apetala by one (K), so K is discarded; MO, JBB and HUEFS go to rule 3.

When two or more names are equally frequent (e.g. one duplicate as Ormosia arborea and one as Ormosia nitida), all of them go to rule 3.


Rule 3: most complete record
Among the remaining records, the one with the most complete information is kept:

records with latitude and longitude are preferred;
then, records with more filled columns;
if records are still tied, the first one in the data is kept.


Block 1: MO has no coordinates and is discarded. JBB and HUEFS both have coordinates, but HUEFS also has the locality, so HUEFS 187321 is kept.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
text:
What is the barRoso?
barRoso is an R package for cleaning, standardizing, and reconciling plant specimen records—especially from biodiversity repositories like GBIF. It streamlines workflows for curators, researchers, and data scientists by automating the harmonization of taxonomic, geographic, and collector metadata. Optimized for reproducibility, barRoso facilitates the detection of duplicate specimens and improves data quality across herbarium datasets.


What can I use barRoso for?

Standardize collector names and associated collector numbers — a crucial step for detecting duplicate specimens across herbaria
Harmonize taxonomic and geographic fields (e.g., family, genus, locality, country)
Detect and flag potential duplicate records using cleaned metadata
Generate herbarium labels from field notebooks, including taxon authority and geolocation maps
Prepare high-quality datasets for biodiversity, floristic, and taxonomic studies



How do I install barRoso?
Follow the Get Started guide for full instructions on installing the package and its dependencies via GitHub.


Is barRoso free to use?
Yes. barRoso is open-source software licensed under the MIT License, which permits unrestricted use, modification, and distribution.


What output can barRoso generate?
While barRoso does not directly produce formatted reports, it supports:

Cleaned and standardized data frames for downstream biodiversity analysis
Visual maps in herbarium label generation
Easy integration with RMarkdown, Quarto, and Shiny for reporting and dashboards



How does barRoso work?
Unlike many packages that rely on static dictionaries to clean collector names, barRoso uses a robust set of regular expressions (regex) to dynamically identify and standardize collector patterns across datasets. This approach allows barRoso to generalize better across sources and spelling variations — even when names are inconsistently formatted. Combined with harmonization of geographic and taxonomic fields, this makes the package especially powerful for detecting duplicates and preparing data for downstream analysis.


Why doesn’t barRoso remove incomplete or inconsistent records?
Because standardization is more powerful than deletion. Many biodiversity records contain valuable metadata even when some fields are missing or messy. barRoso standardizes and flags potential problems but leaves the final decision to the user—preserving data integrity and maximizing research potential.


Who are the developers of barRoso?
Development is sponsored by JBRJ, FINEP, and CNPq. Main developer:

Domingos Cardoso (@DBOSlab)

View the code and contribute on GitHub: https://github.com/DBOSlab/barRoso


Why the name barRoso?
The name honors Graziela Maciel Barroso (1912–2003), a pioneering Brazilian botanist. It also serves as an acronym: Biodiversity Analysis and Record Reconciliation for Organizing Specimen Observations, highlighting both its mission and its deep roots in the R programming ecosystem.


Where can I report bugs or request features?
Submit issues on GitHub: barRoso Issues.


Where can I ask questions or join the community?
Visit GitHub Discussions to ask questions, share ideas, or connect with other users.

title: Format Datasets into Darwin Core
text:
Overview
Herbarium records downloaded from different portals rarely share the same column names and formats. GBIF uses Darwin Core terms such as recordedBy and decimalLatitude, while a speciesLink download may call them collector and latitude, write dates as 23/11/2011, or keep the year, month and day of identification in separate columns.
The function barroso_dwc() formats a dataset into Darwin Core column names and value formats, so records from GBIF, speciesLink, REFLORA and JABOT can be combined and standardized together. It recognizes the source of the data by itself.

title: Format Datasets into Darwin Core
text:
Usage
library(barRoso)

splink <- readxl::read_excel("speciesLink-20260409091223-0027073.xlsx", col_types = "text")

splink <- barroso_dwc(splink)
#> barroso_dwc: speciesLink format; renamed 20 columns (collector -> recordedBy,
#> collectornumber -> recordNumber, yearcollected -> year, monthcollected -> month, ...);
#> renamed 13 columns (basisofrecord -> basisOfRecord, stateprovince -> stateProvince, ...);
#> cleaned 3097 specificEpithet (e.g. "cf. platychila", "sp. 2"); created dateIdentified
#> from year, month and day of identification; added the author to 133418 scientificName;
#> took 1585 missing recordNumber from fieldNumber; created species from genus and
#> specificEpithet
The report tells what was changed. The source can also be given explicitly:
splink <- barroso_dwc(splink, source = "speciesLink")   # also "REFLORA", "JABOT", "GBIF"
You don’t need to call barroso_dwc() before barroso_cat(): it formats each source by itself before combining them.
combined <- barroso_cat(list(GBIF = gbif, speciesLink = splink), keep_source = "GBIF")
All columns are returned as character, so the outputs of different downloads can always be combined. For example, when querying several species with plantR::rspeciesLink(), a column like coordinatePrecision may come as integer for one species and as character for another, and dplyr::bind_rows() would fail:
data_speciesLink <- lapply(targeted_taxa, function(x) {
  splink <- plantR::rspeciesLink(key = personal_key, species = x, save = FALSE)
  barroso_dwc(splink)
})
names(data_speciesLink) <- targeted_taxa
data_speciesLink <- dplyr::bind_rows(data_speciesLink, .id = "original_search")
Use as_character = FALSE to keep the original column types.

title: Fix and Flag Coordinates
text:
Overview
Geographic coordinates of herbarium specimens often have errors: latitude and longitude swapped, a missing minus sign, coordinates pointing to the herbarium that houses the specimen or to the center of a country, or just too few decimals. The function std_coordinates() checks the coordinates following the workflow of the bdc package and, in line with the barRoso philosophy, it fixes what can be safely fixed and flags everything else, so you know what was changed and which records need attention.

title: Fix and Flag Coordinates
text:
Installation of the suggested packages
std_coordinates() uses packages that are not installed with barRoso by default:
install.packages(c("bdc", "CoordinateCleaner", "rnaturalearth", "rnaturalearthdata"))
install.packages("rnaturalearthhires", repos = "https://ropensci.r-universe.dev")

title: Fix and Flag Coordinates
text:
Usage
library(barRoso)

df <- read.csv("gbif.csv")

df_coords <- std_coordinates(df)

# What was fixed or flagged
table(unlist(strsplit(df_coords$coordinateIssues, "; ")))
Custom column names can be given, e.g. for raw speciesLink downloads:
df_coords <- std_coordinates(splink,
                             colname_decimalLatitude = "latitude",
                             colname_decimalLongitude = "longitude",
                             colname_scientificName = "scientificname")

title: Fix and Flag Coordinates
text:
What is checked
The checks are applied in this order:









Step
Check
Based on
Result




1
Coordinates stored as text, e.g. "-12,5" with decimal comma, or "Bloqueada" in speciesLink
—
converted into numbers; values that are not numbers are set to NA and flagged


2
Empty coordinates
bdc::bdc_coordinates_empty()
flagged


3

bdc::bdc_coordinates_outOfRange()
flagged


4
Latitude and longitude transposed, or with inverted signs
bdc::bdc_coordinates_transposed()
fixed


5
Coordinates outside the country informed in the record
bdc::bdc_coordinates_country_inconsistent()
flagged


6
Low precision, i.e. fewer decimals than min_decimals (default: 2)
bdc::bdc_coordinates_precision()
flagged


7
Country capitals, country and province centroids, biodiversity institutions, zero or equal coordinates, and the GBIF headquarters
CoordinateCleaner::clean_coordinates(), as in the space module of bdc
flagged



Country names are standardized with bdc::bdc_country_standardized() just for these checks; the country column of your data is not changed.

Transposed coordinates
A record is tested when its coordinates fall outside its country (considering a buffer of 0.2 degrees). As in bdc, seven combinations are tried, in this order, and the first one falling inside the country is kept:

sign of latitude inverted
sign of longitude inverted
signs of latitude and longitude inverted
latitude and longitude swapped
latitude and longitude swapped, and sign of latitude inverted
latitude and longitude swapped, and sign of longitude inverted
latitude and longitude swapped, and signs inverted

For example, a record from Brazil at latitude 10.2 and longitude -59.35 falls in the Atlantic Ocean; with the sign of the latitude inverted (-10.2), it falls in Brazil, so it is fixed.






Note



The steps 4 and 5 follow the same logic of the corresponding bdc functions (same Natural Earth map, buffers and combinations), but are run by barRoso itself. In bdc 1.1.6, bdc_coordinates_transposed() writes the fixed coordinates back into the wrong records when several countries are corrected at once, and bdc_coordinates_country_inconsistent() fails or flags correct coordinates with recent versions of dplyr.




Coordinates outside the informed country
Coordinates are flagged when they fall outside the country informed in the record, considering a buffer of 0.1 degrees to avoid flagging records close to the borders or on the coast.

section: Coordinates in degrees, minutes and seconds
text:
Coordinates in degrees, minutes and seconds
Herbarium labels and the verbatim coordinates of databases like REFLORA and JABOT are often written in degrees, minutes and seconds. The function dms_to_decimal() converts them into decimal degrees, recognizing the many symbols and hemisphere letters found in herbarium data, also in Portuguese (O for oeste, L for leste):
dms_to_decimal(c("22º22´55´´S", "53°45'W", "12 30 15.5 S", "S 8°30.5'", "43º40'49''O", "-55.602222"))
#> [1] -22.381944 -53.750000 -12.504306  -8.508333 -43.680278 -55.602222
When the hemisphere is not written, as in many REFLORA latitudes (e.g. "22º22´55´´"), it can be given:
dms_to_decimal(reflora$verbatimLatitude, type = "latitude", hemisphere = "S")
Invalid values, like "60º6´61´´W" (61 seconds) or latitudes beyond 90°, become NA with a warning. Checked against 423 REFLORA and JABOT records that have both verbatim and decimal coordinates, all valid values match the decimal coordinates of the databases.
Unlike std_coordinates(), dms_to_decimal() works on a single vector of coordinates, so it can be used before checking the coordinates:
df$decimalLatitude <- dms_to_decimal(df$verbatimLatitude, type = "latitude")
df$decimalLongitude <- dms_to_decimal(df$verbatimLongitude, type = "longitude")
df <- std_coordinates(df)

title: Standardize Specimen Records
text:
Overview
The barroso_std() function is the primary tool in the barRoso package for performing full data cleaning and standardization of biodiversity specimen records. It is designed to process raw data from herbaria, virtual repositories, and field collections, ensuring harmonized fields across taxonomic, geographic, and collector-related information.

title: Standardize Specimen Records
text:
Key Features

Normalize collector names and collection numbers
Normalize determiner names (identifiedBy)
Standardize geographic fields like country, state, and locality
Harmonize taxonomic names including family, genus, and species
Clean and normalize type status
Optionally remove unvouchered or duplicate records
Support for multilingual column names (e.g., Portuguese, Spanish)

Usage
library(barRoso)

df <- read.csv("raw_herbarium_data.csv")

                               unvouchered = TRUE,
                               delunkcoll = FALSE,
                               flag_missid = TRUE,
                               flag_duplicates = TRUE,
                               rm_duplicates = FALSE,
                               colname_recordedBy = "recordedBy",
                               colname_recordNumber = "recordNumber",
                               colname_identifiedBy = "identifiedBy",
                               colname_country = "country",
                               colname_stateProvince = "stateProvince",
                               colname_county = "county",
                               colname_municipality = "municipality",
                               colname_locality = "locality",
                               colname_collectionCode = "collectionCode",
                               colname_institutionCode = "institutionCode",
                               colname_typeStatus = "typeStatus",

title: About barRoso
text:
Overview
barRoso (Biodiversity Analysis and Record Reconciliation for Organizing Specimen Observations) is an R package that streamlines biodiversity data cleaning, integration, and reconciliation, particularly for herbarium records. The toolkit supports workflows from data curation to label production, helping botanists, curators, and researchers analyze plant specimen collections more efficiently.
Named in honor of Graziela Maciel Barroso, one of Brazil’s most respected botanists, the name barRoso also nods to its native programming environment—R.
The package was originally developed for the JABOT Virtual Herbarium, maintained by the Rio de Janeiro Botanical Garden, but it is generalizable to other biodiversity repositories such as GBIF, SEINet, REFLORA, and speciesLink. The package was originally developed to support the cleaning and reconciliation of plant specimen records retrieved from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF), but its flexible design makes it broadly applicable to other biodiversity data sources. These include national and institutional repositories such as the JABOT Virtual Herbarium, maintained by the Rio de Janeiro Botanical Garden and REFLORA, as well as SEINet and speciesLink.

title: Overview
text:
What is barRoso?
barRoso is an R package designed to clean, standardize, and reconcile plant specimen records, especially those retrieved from herbarium databases and biodiversity repositories. Originally developed for GBIF, it is compatible with data from JABOT, SEINet, REFLORA, speciesLink, and others.
The package is named after Brazilian botanist Graziela Maciel Barroso, and also serves as an acronym: Biodiversity Analysis and Record Reconciliation for Organizing Specimen Observations.

title: Overview
text:
What does barRoso do?
barRoso helps users:

Standardize collector and determiner names and collection numbers using regex-based parsing
Harmonize taxonomic, geographic, and temporal fields
Combine records from GBIF, speciesLink and other sources
Flag and remove potential duplicates across herbarium records, highlighting conflicting identifications
Fix and flag geographic coordinates, following the workflow of the bdc package
Generate herbarium labels from fieldbook data
Write lists of examined specimens in the format of 17 botanical journals
Integrate with external taxonomic databases (e.g., LCVP, WFO)
Prepare large-scale biodiversity datasets for publication and analysis

title: Overview
text:
Who should use barRoso?

Taxonomists and herbarium curators
Biodiversity data scientists
Floristic inventory teams
Graduate students and researchers managing field collections

title: Overview
text:
What makes barRoso different?
Unlike other packages that rely on static collector name dictionaries, barRoso uses robust, extensible regular expressions to detect name patterns and correct inconsistencies across data sources. It also includes modular, tidyverse-compatible functions for a reproducible and efficient workflow.

title: Overview
text:
Data Preservation Philosophy
While many data tools prioritize aggressive cleaning, often at the cost of discarding valuable records, barRoso takes a different approach. Its philosophy centers on standardization rather than removal. All herbarium specimens carry potential scientific value, even when incomplete or inconsistently entered. Instead of omitting such records, barRoso focuses on harmonizing fields to enhance comparability across collections. By standardizing collector names, geographic fields, and taxonomic labels, barRoso allows users to flag rather than erase inconsistencies, enabling more transparent workflows and tracing potential misidentifications, especially across distributed duplicates. This inclusive approach honors the archival role of herbaria while facilitating reproducible biodiversity research.
